expert.item: Writes go through a write-ahead log before (or alongside) landing in the memtable, so a crash before flush doesn't lose data.
The memtable is an in-memory sorted structure; RocksDB's default implementation is a skiplist.
A full memtable becomes immutable; a new mutable memtable takes writes while the immutable one waits in the flush pipeline (memtable pipelining).
Flushing writes the immutable memtable out as one new, sorted, immutable SSTable file, sequentially, at the newest level (L0).
A point read checks the newest structure first and stops at the first match: the active memtable, then immutable memtables, then SSTables from newest to oldest.
A per-file Bloom filter lets a read skip an SSTable without touching disk: hash the key, probe those bits, and a single zero bit proves the key is absent from that file.
A Bloom filter can be wrong in only one direction: it never gives a false negative, but it can give a false positive, forcing a wasted read of a file that doesn't actually hold the key.
After a Bloom filter passes, a per-file block index (a binary-search structure over that file's data blocks) finds the one data block that might hold the key, without scanning the whole file.
A range read can't stop at the first match: it must scan every live structure's overlap with the range and merge the results (newest version of each key wins), typically via a priority queue.
A delete is written as a new record, a tombstone, not an in-place removal; it occupies real space on disk until a later compaction discards it.
Compaction is what actually removes tombstones and superseded duplicate keys by merging files down the levels; it is the next topic's own mechanism, not re-taught here.
Two merge policies (levelling vs tiering) trade write amplification against read cost; which to pick, and the RUM conjecture itself, belongs to the compaction topic.
The skip list's own structure (how a skip list is built and searched) is assumed background from the Data Structures & Algorithms track, not re-taught here.
Partitioned and block-based (old-format) Bloom filter variants, and the exact false-positive-rate math, are implementation detail beyond what this topic's outcomes need.
expert.out: too deep for this topic's outcomes; the single full-filter rejection/false-positive measurement is enough to teach the mechanism
